title: Smart Honeypot System for Analyzing Zero-Day Attacks
shortDesc: A honeypot simulating SSH, FTP, HTTP, Telnet and SMB services to capture and analyze attacker behavior in real time.
features: Simulates SSH, FTP, HTTP, Telnet and SMB services to capture attacker activity
Real-time dashboard for monitoring attacks, protocols, and threat statistics
IP reputation analysis, anomaly detection, and GeoIP tracking
Automated threat scoring
Generates security reports in CSV, JSON and PDF formats
challenges: Building a real-time dashboard that could reflect live attacker sessions without blocking the honeypot services required moving event delivery onto WebSockets via Django Channels backed by Redis as the channel layer.
learnings: Gained hands-on experience with asynchronous Python (Django Channels), designing services that intentionally expose themselves as attack surfaces, and turning raw connection logs into structured threat intelligence.
futureImprovements: Add more emulated services, integrate a real threat-intel feed for IP reputation, and containerize the system with Docker for easier deployment.

title: PDF Malware Analysis Toolkit
shortDesc: A static analysis toolkit that inspects PDF files for embedded threats, malicious JavaScript, and indicators of compromise.
features: Static PDF malware analysis using PDFiD and peepdf
Extracts metadata, embedded JavaScript, and embedded objects
Identifies Indicators of Compromise (IOCs)
Generates automated risk scores
Produces structured malware analysis reports
challenges: PDF files can hide malicious content across nested objects and obfuscated JavaScript streams, so correctly parsing the object structure without executing anything was the core challenge.
learnings: Learned how PDF malware typically hides payloads (auto-actions, embedded JS, obfuscated streams) and how to build a scoring system that reflects real risk rather than just flagging keywords.
futureImprovements: Integrate YARA rule updates automatically and add a sandboxed dynamic analysis mode for deeper inspection.

title: Process Monitor Agent
shortDesc: A lightweight Windows agent that watches running processes, flags suspicious behavior, and raises real-time alerts.
features: Continuous Windows process monitoring using psutil
Detects suspicious process behavior
Structured activity logging
Real-time alerts for endpoint monitoring
challenges: Distinguishing genuinely suspicious process behavior from normal system noise required tuning detection heuristics to keep false positives low.
learnings: Built a practical understanding of endpoint monitoring fundamentals and how SOC tooling turns raw OS-level signals into actionable alerts.
futureImprovements: Add a central logging endpoint so multiple agents can report to one dashboard, and expand detection heuristics.

title: Following a Web Connection with Wireshark
shortDesc: Traced a browser connection end-to-end using packet evidence: DNS resolution, TCP handshake, and TLS Client Hello (SNI).
features: Captured and filtered live traffic to isolate a single web connection from background noise
Correlated a DNS query/response with the resulting TCP handshake and TLS session to the same IP
Identified the TLS Client Hello's SNI field as evidence of intended destination despite encryption
Observed QUIC (HTTP/3) traffic alongside fallback TCP/TLS, reflecting modern browser behavior
challenges: Isolating one connection's traffic from a mix of background browser activity (telemetry, other domains) required building increasingly specific display filters, starting from a broad DNS query filter down to an exact IP match.
learnings: Learned to reconstruct what a system connected to using only network metadata (DNS records, TCP handshake, SNI) — the same class of evidence available even when payloads are encrypted, and foundational to spotting abnormal connections later.
futureImprovements: Extend the exercise to a suspicious/malicious PCAP sample to practice distinguishing normal baseline traffic from an anomalous connection.

title: Investigating Windows Processes with Sysmon
shortDesc: Installed Sysmon and used Event ID 1 (Process Create) telemetry to reconstruct what ran, who ran it, and what launched it.
features: Installed Sysmon with default configuration to capture process-creation telemetry
Generated and located known-good baseline events (Notepad, whoami via PowerShell) in Event Viewer
Analyzed Image, CommandLine, User, ParentImage and timestamp fields for each event
Explained why parent-child process relationships (e.g. PowerShell spawned from explorer.exe vs. from Word) are a key triage signal
challenges: With 170+ events generated during a normal session, finding the exact events tied to deliberately generated activity required using Event Viewer's Find function rather than manually scrolling.
learnings: Sysmon doesn't decide what's malicious — it records evidence. The same alert (e.g. 'powershell.exe executed') can be completely routine or highly suspicious depending on the process's command line, parent process, and user context.
futureImprovements: Build a small set of custom Sysmon rules to reduce noise and highlight only high-signal parent-child relationships (e.g. Office apps spawning shells).

title: The Urgent Materials Payment — BEC Investigation
shortDesc: Investigated a business email compromise attempt: a lookalike-domain vendor impersonation requesting an urgent $18,740 payment.
features: Verified case file integrity via SHA-256 hash before analysis
Compared sender and Reply-To domains against the approved vendor domain on file
Identified a lookalike sending domain and a third, different Reply-To domain
Explained why SPF/DKIM/DMARC all passing does not clear a lookalike-domain BEC attempt
Documented social-engineering indicators: urgency and discouraged verification
challenges: The email had no attachment, malware, or malicious link — the entire investigation rested on domain comparison and header analysis rather than any technical artifact to detonate or scan.
learnings: SPF/DKIM/DMARC only prove a message came from the domain it claims — not that the domain has any relationship with the organization. This is exactly why lookalike-domain BEC routinely passes all three checks.
futureImprovements: Practice the same workflow against a sample using domain homoglyphs (e.g. rn vs m) to sharpen visual domain-comparison skills.

title: The Failed Login Alert — First SIEM Investigation with Wazuh
shortDesc: Deployed Wazuh SIEM, connected an endpoint agent, and investigated a controlled failed-then-successful login sequence.
features: Deployed the official Wazuh virtual appliance and networked it with a Windows endpoint
Installed and verified an active Wazuh agent on the monitored endpoint
Generated a controlled failed->failed->failed->successful authentication sequence
Correlated Event ID 4625 (failed logon) and 4624 (successful logon) into a timeline
Wrote a Tier 1 case note with a false-positive disposition and escalation criteria
challenges: Getting the Wazuh VM and Windows host to communicate required configuring a bridged network adapter so both machines could reach each other on the local network, and waiting through the appliance's multi-minute dashboard initialization.
learnings: A SIEM's core value is correlation speed — a single filtered search surfaced count, timing and MITRE ATT&CK context instantly. But the SIEM never makes the judgment call: the same alert wording can mean something routine or something serious depending on source, volume and account context.
futureImprovements: Add a second monitored endpoint to practice distinguishing single-host failed logins from a pattern spread across multiple machines (a stronger brute-force indicator).

title: Defender Found Something — Endpoint Alert Triage
shortDesc: Triaged an EICAR test-file detection end-to-end: Microsoft Defender's response, Windows Event Viewer, and Wazuh SIEM correlation.
features: Configured the Wazuh agent to forward Windows Defender's Operational event log via a custom eventchannel block
Generated a real Defender detection using the industry-standard EICAR test file
Verified Defender's automated Quarantine action via Event ID 1116/1117 in Event Viewer
Correlated the exact same detection independently in Wazuh (Rule 62123, Level 12)
Wrote a full incident record plus an optional Tier 2 escalation handoff
challenges: The first EICAR test was run before the Defender eventchannel config change and agent restart, so Wazuh never received it — Wazuh only forwards events generated after it starts monitoring a log source, not historical backfill. Re-running the test after the config change resolved it.
learnings: A config with no errors doesn't guarantee data is flowing — confirming an event actually arrived in the SIEM is itself part of the verification work, not just writing a config block correctly.
futureImprovements: Configure a Wazuh active response to automatically isolate a host on a high-severity Defender detection, and document the resulting workflow.
